title: Al-'Aliyy, the Most High
tomorrow: Allahu akbar: greater than what, exactly?

lines: GLORY TO MY LORD, THE MOST HIGH.
cards: The week before something big: a recital, a final, a wedding, a move. The list keeps scrolling behind your eyes at night, and every item feels like it sits on your chest. Yesterday's question meets that weight.

Why do Muslims say 'Most High' with their foreheads on the floor? In sujud, the prostration, the head goes lower than the heart, and the words are subhana rabbiyal a'la: glory to my Lord, the Most High.

teach.h: PRAISE THY LORD THE MOST HIGH.
teach.b: Remember the hadith about the bow: when a verse came down about the Magnificent, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, put it in your ruku'. Here's its second half.
When the verse came down that says, in Pickthall's words, "Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High," the Prophet said: put it in your sujud. So the lowest posture carries the highest Name.
That's today's: Al-'Aliyy, the Most High, above everything, nothing over Him. And here's the line to tell a friend tonight.

In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet said the closest a servant comes to his Lord is while prostrating, so ask a lot in it. The Most High, and you closest to Him with your face on the ground. Height isn't a distance here.
It's a direction. Everything you set down on the floor in sujud is set down before the one above all of it.
So when someone tells you, the night the list won't stop scrolling, to take it to the floor, it isn't about making it smaller.
To put it under the one who is higher than it, and say so out loud.

how: In each sujud of the prayer, Muslims say subhana rabbiyal a'la, glory to my Lord the Most High; personal du'a is also made in sujud, following the hadith that a servant is closest to Allah while prostrating.

o: the one who lives at the top of the sky
the one who stays far from people
the Most High, above all things

games.q: the floor and its words — tap the pairs.
p: glory to my Lord, the Most High
what the Prophet said of the verse

s: in sujud you're at the lowest point, so the farthest from God
the closest a servant comes to his Lord is while prostrating, the Prophet said.
the words said in sujud trace back to a verse, like the words in ruku'
"Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High": put it in your sujud.

games.q: your friend says she can't pray while she's this anxious; she'll wait until she's calm and focused. what does the sujud hadith suggest?
o: wait; prayer only counts with a calm, focused mind.
bring it now; a servant is closest in sujud, so ask a lot there.
skip the prayer and just think positive thoughts instead.
games.why: the Prophet said to ask a lot in sujud, because a servant is closest there. the anxious list is exactly what goes on the floor.

practice: If you pray, you can make one sujud now, forehead to the floor, and say subhana rabbiyal a'la, slowly, and stay there a moment. If not, sit and fold forward, letting your head drop toward your knees.
Either way, name the heaviest thing on your list and set it down below you for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Aliyy. The Most High, praised from the lowest place, closest there.

orig.note: Arabic: the Most High. in sujud, the verse's al-a'la: subhana rabbiyal a'la.

carryVoice: The line to keep: most high, so the heaviest thing can go on the floor. Rest well tonight.

sources.q: Praise the name of thy Lord the Most High,

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 869; Sunan Ibn Majah 887 ('Uqbah ibn 'Amir: put it in your sujud)
sources.work: Sunan Abi Dawud; Sunan Ibn Majah

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 482 (the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so make much du'a)
